prompt: Each card shows a consumer thinking about a purchase. Is the consumer using fast, automatic System 1 or slow, deliberate System 2?

cards.text: Amir spots the familiar orange logo of his usual crackers and drops a box into the cart without slowing down.
cards.explanation: System 1: recognizing a familiar logo happens in an instant and without effort.

cards.text: Leila turns into a shop the moment she sees a large red banner in the window.
cards.explanation: System 1: reacting to a sale sign is fast and automatic.

cards.text: On a busy weekday, Tom grabs the same carton of milk he always buys.
cards.explanation: System 1: most everyday purchases rely on fast, automatic thinking.

cards.text: Rosa divides the price of each detergent bottle by its number of washes before choosing.
cards.explanation: System 2: comparing the price per unit is slow, deliberate, and effortful.

cards.text: Before signing a car lease, Ken reads every clause about fees and penalties.
cards.explanation: System 2: reading the terms of a contract takes deliberate effort, and the decision is important.

cards.text: Mina sees a jacket priced far below what she expected, stops, and checks the label and reviews to find out why.
cards.explanation: System 2 overrides System 1 when the consumer detects a clear anomaly and has the time and capacity to analyze it.

prompt: Each consumer takes a mental shortcut. Which heuristic is it?

cases.text: After a week of news stories about lost luggage, Dev decides that checking a bag on his airline is very risky.
cases.explanation: Availability heuristic: recent vivid examples come easily to mind, so Dev overestimates the frequency of the risk.

cases.text: A supermarket cola in a red can with white script seems to Luis as good as the leading national brand.
cases.explanation: Representativeness heuristic: the can resembles the category prototype, so it seems to share its quality.

cases.text: Because her friend was recently overcharged by a phone repair shop, Pia believes most repair shops overcharge.
cases.explanation: Availability heuristic: one vivid example that comes easily to mind makes the event seem common.

cases.text: A cereal box with green leaves and a farm drawing seems healthy to Ada because it looks like the organic brands she knows.
cases.explanation: Representativeness heuristic: the box resembles a familiar category prototype, so Ada judges it as belonging to it.

question_text: A furniture store places a $2,400 sofa at the entrance, beside the $1,100 sofa it most wants to sell. Which explanation fits what the slide describes?
hint: Think about what an initial reference number does to a later valuation.
correct_answer_citation: Week 8: Anchoring and Arbitrary Reference Numbers

options.option_text: The $2,400 sofa will sell best, because consumers always purchase the highest-priced item in a store
options.option_explanation: The store's aim here is to shift the reference point used to judge the $1,100 sofa.

options.option_text: The first price has no effect, because consumers ignore numbers that are not relevant to their final choice
options.option_explanation: Anchoring occurs even when the initial number is arbitrary or inflated.

options.option_text: The $2,400 price acts as an anchor that makes $1,100 seem lower than it would on its own
options.option_explanation: Correct. An initial reference number pulls subsequent price judgments toward it, making the $1,100 price seem more acceptable.

options.option_text: Consumers will compare every sofa in the store and choose without reference to starting numbers
options.option_explanation: That describes the neoclassical utility model rather than anchoring and adjustment.

prompt: Each card describes a consumer's reaction. Does it illustrate loss aversion directly or the endowment effect?

cards.text: A $30 parking fine ruins Sara's day, whereas a $30 rebate the week before barely lifted her mood.
cards.explanation: Loss aversion: a $30 loss inflicts roughly twice as much disutility as a $30 gain provides pleasure.

cards.text: Ben refuses to sell a coffee mug he was given for $10, even though he would never have paid more than $5 to acquire it.
cards.explanation: Endowment effect: once Ben owns the mug, giving it up is coded as a loss, raising the value he assigns to it.

cards.text: Nadia feels the $50 her portfolio lost far more intensely than the $50 it gained the month before.
cards.explanation: Loss aversion: the value function is steeper in the domain of losses than in the domain of gains.

cards.text: After a 30-day free trial of a music service, Theo pays to keep it because canceling feels like losing his library.
cards.explanation: Endowment effect: possession during the free trial shifts the reference point so giving the service up feels like a loss.

cards.text: Kim demands far more for her used armchair than prospective buyers are willing to pay for an identical chair.
cards.explanation: Endowment effect: ownership elevates the seller's valuation above the buyer's willingness to pay.

cards.text: Raj refuses a fair coin toss in which he would win $50 on heads or lose $50 on tails.
cards.explanation: Loss aversion: losing $50 hurts roughly twice as much as winning $50 pleases.

question_text: A retailer considers two one-cent price reductions on a coffee maker: lowering the price from $50.00 to $49.99, or lowering it from $49.99 to $49.98. According to the left-digit effect, which reduction lowers perceived price magnitude more?
hint: Think about how System 1 reads prices from left to right and which digit changes.
correct_answer_citation: Week 8: Just-Below Pricing and the Left-Digit Effect

options.option_text: Lowering the price from $50.00 to $49.99, because the leftmost digit drops from 5 to 4
options.option_explanation: Correct. Because consumers anchor disproportionately on the leftmost digit when reading left to right, changing the left digit produces a much larger drop in perceived price.

options.option_text: Lowering the price from $49.99 to $49.98, because 8 is an even digit
options.option_explanation: The leftmost digits (49) remain unchanged between $49.99 and $49.98.

options.option_text: Both reductions have the exact same effect on perceived price because both equal one cent
options.option_explanation: Under System 1 left-digit encoding, a one-cent drop that changes the left digit has a much larger perceptual impact.

options.option_text: Neither reduction affects perception unless the price is rounded to $45.00
options.option_explanation: Just-below pricing specifically relies on dropping one cent below a round number to change the leftmost digit.

prompt: Each case describes how options are arranged for a decision maker. Is it a default option or a nudge that changes option placement?

cases.text: New employees are automatically enrolled in a retirement savings plan unless they submit a form to opt out.
cases.explanation: Default option: automatic enrollment is the outcome that takes effect if the employee takes no active step.

cases.text: A cafeteria moves bottled water and fruit to eye level while keeping sugary sodas on the bottom shelf at the same price.
cases.explanation: Nudge: altering option placement steers behavior toward healthier choices without forbidding any option or changing prices.

cases.text: A utility provider assigns every new household to the renewable electricity tier unless the household selects another tier.
cases.explanation: Default option: customers who take no action receive the pre-selected renewable tier.

cases.text: An office building places prominent footprints leading to the staircase while leaving the elevator accessible nearby.
cases.explanation: Nudge: visual cues in the environment steer behavior in the chooser's interest without restricting alternatives.

question_text: In controlled experiments where all product attributes and prices were simultaneously visible on the screen, how did most frontier AI shopping agents respond to a $4.99 just-below price and a promotional discount frame (Wadi & Ma, 2026b)?
hint: Compare human System 1 left-digit illusions against how AI agents weighted cents and discounts under full information.
correct_answer_citation: Week 8: How AI Agents Respond to Just-Below Pricing and Promotional Framing

options.option_text: Every AI agent ignored the .99 cents component and treated $4.99 as $4.00
options.option_explanation: Under full information, seven of eight tested AI agents weighted the cents component equally with the whole-dollar component.

options.option_text: Most AI agents weighted cents equally with whole dollars and weighted discount savings identically to list-price reductions
options.option_explanation: Correct. When all numbers were directly visible, seven of eight agents showed no left-digit illusion and six of eight showed no transaction-utility distortion.

options.option_text: AI agents refused to buy any product priced at $4.99 because charm pricing was flagged as deceptive
options.option_explanation: Agents evaluated the prices arithmetically rather than rejecting charm-priced items.

options.option_text: AI agents valued a dollar saved through a promotional discount three times as much as a lower list price
options.option_explanation: Six of eight tested agents weighted a promotional discount dollar identically to a list-price reduction.
